bugs.description: Buffer overflow and missing null terminator in copy_string(). The function copies bytes without bounds checking and never writes a null terminator, leading to potential buffer overflow and unterminated string reads.
Division by zero: safe_divide() does not check if the divisor 'b' is zero. This causes undefined behavior (SIGFPE crash on most platforms) when called with b=0.
Null pointer dereference: alloc_buffer() calls memset on the result of malloc without checking for NULL. If malloc fails (out of memory), memset dereferences NULL causing a segfault.

Signed integer overflow: parse_int() accumulates digits in an int without overflow checking. For large numeric strings, the multiplication 'result * 10' overflows INT_MAX, causing undefined behavior per C standard.

Race condition on shared state: connection_count is read and modified without synchronization. In a multi-threaded environment, concurrent calls can exceed max_connections or corrupt the count. Requires mutex protection.

Stack buffer overflow in send_data(): memcpy copies 'len' bytes into a 256-byte stack buffer without checking if len > 256. A caller passing data larger than 256 bytes corrupts the stack, enabling potential code execution via return address overwrite.

Off-by-one out-of-bounds write: buffer[bytes_read] writes at index buf_size, which is one past the end of the allocated buffer. This corrupts adjacent memory, potentially overwriting control data or causing segfaults.

Resource leak and underflow: close_connection() never calls close() on the socket file descriptor, leaking the OS resource. Also decrements connection_count without checking > 0, which can cause unsigned underflow if called more times than connect.

Format string vulnerability: user-controlled input is passed directly as the format string to printf(). An attacker can use %x, %n format specifiers to read/write arbitrary memory, leading to information disclosure or code execution.

Two bugs: (1) strcpy with no length check overflows the 64-byte name buffer for long inputs. (2) No bounds check on user_count before indexing users[], allowing array out-of-bounds write when MAX_USERS is exceeded.

Use-after-free and double-free: When strlen(buffer) > 100, the buffer is freed but execution continues to printf() which reads freed memory (use-after-free), then free() is called again (double-free). Both are undefined behavior exploitable for arbitrary code execution.

File handle leak: read_config() opens a file but returns -2 on the ERROR path without calling fclose(). Each leaked FILE* consumes a file descriptor, eventually causing fopen() to fail system-wide when the fd limit is reached.
Unbounded input: scanf("%s") reads until whitespace with no length limit, overflowing the 1024-byte input buffer. Use fgets() with explicit size limit to prevent stack buffer overflow.

Cross-module buffer overflow: copy_string() in utils.c has no bounds checking, and main.c passes unbounded user input through it into a 128-byte buffer allocated by alloc_buffer(). An attacker can overflow the heap buffer via the input string.

Cross-module buffer overflow: send_data() in network.c copies data into a 256-byte stack buffer without length validation. main.c passes user-controlled data of arbitrary length, allowing stack buffer overflow and potential code execution.
